content.title: Reviewers, thank you for improving our paper!
content.comment:
Dear reviewers,

*Thank you so much* for your very valuable comments on our paper! We realize the paper may not be in its best shape for ICLR. Therefore, after a hard time of considering, we decide to withdraw this paper. This said, your time has not been wasted -- your precious suggestions will be well-taken when we revise the paper to a better version. Thank you!

Sincerely,

Authors

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper takes another look at the debate between whether there is any value to retain the pretrained weights for filter pruning or whether it is better to train from scratch. The key contributions of this paper are (1) existing works did not explore hyperparameters like learning rate in sufficient detail, and (2) another method to establish approximate isometry (the authors claim exact isometry but only linear network experiments are provided).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper has following strengths:

1. Observation that other existing papers did not explore a higher learning rate is useful.
2. Paper is well-written.


The paper has following weaknesses:

1. I am not convinced that training from scratch is sufficiently outperformed by finetuning with higher learning rate. Clearly, the finetuning with higher LR outperforms finetuning with lower LR. However, if the authors’ claims on outperforming “training from scratch” results hold, we should have seen the most impact in high pruning ratio regimes (we currently see opposite trend for high pruning ratios: scratch outperforms finetuning methods). In many other cases also, the differences between “scratch” and “finetuning with high LR” (Table 2) is like 0.2-0.4% which is not sufficient to demonstrate conclusive results. Specifically, there is probably no easy way to know if the “scratch” case could not have been improved by any other LR, weight decay, or other hyperparameter setting. Given that the authors are playing around with hyperparameters like LR to improve their pruning results, one can do the same thing for “scratch” results and potentially obtain different trends altogether. I do not have a solution for the above problem. This is probably one of the major challenges for conducting “fair” comparisons in deep learning. Most new methods/papers come up with their own set of hyperparameters which is indeed a problem for the research community. Hence, while I appreciate authors’ initiative to conduct more thorough and fair comparisons, I still think there may be more discrepancies due to learning rate in their Table 1/2 results.

2. I am not sure if I understood how “Fair-Setup-1” is actually fair? Aren’t you training with a higher learning rate for a longer duration (even if the total epochs are the same)? If so, it is not surprising that this method achieved better results than “scratch”. When the LR decay schedule is also fixed, it is not conclusive that “Fair-Setup-2” is actually significantly better than “scratch”. For example, for 0.3, 0.9, 0.95 pruning ratios, the std dev of “scratch” is very high and in some cases matches the range achieved by “Fair-Setup-2”. This is also done for 100 classes in ImageNet. On the full imagenet setup, this difference will likely disappear.

3. It is not a new result that initialization is the key or that establishing exact/approximate isometry will help. This is pointed out by the authors themselves (and was discussed at length in Lee et al, 2020 paper). Although the authors point out differences between this work and Lee et al, 2020, the contributions are not novel enough. Specifically, the main contributions are: (a) authors tried out higher learning rate when finetuning a pruned model, and (b) they created a new method for establishing isometry for filter pruning (as opposed to unstructured pruning as done by Lee et al, 2020). The contribution (b) could have been very interesting if they had shown large-scale or SotA results for their newly proposed technique. Unfortunately, the authors provided results only for a linear network with MNIST.

4. Box on page 8: Authors claim that *they show* (e.g., see phrases like “following plausible explanations”) that a higher LR fixes the dynamical isometry better. However, this is purely based on empirical results in the main paper and appendix A.4, that too on a toy dataset and a linear network. Please refrain from making such claims unless you can theoretically show that larger LR actually makes the mean singular values go towards 1. While I can empirically see this for the toy experiment, the paper doesn’t actually show *how* or *why* a higher LR would result in better gradient properties in the pruned model.

5. Some lacking related work: There are other follow up works that connected dynamical isometry to architecture properties (e.g., presence of skip connections, depth, width, etc.). For example, see [Bhardwaj et al., 2021] (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.00780). This work can be seen as a filter pruning (or more generally as architecture design in a training-free way) as they directly change depth and width of the model to discover compressed networks. They also present theory connecting dynamical isometry to these architectural characteristics, along with concrete experimental validation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Paper is well-written but not novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper’s results are not conclusive enough. Part of the problem is missing hyperparameter tuning for their main comparison point (which in itself can be very challenging for deep learning models). Other part is the lack of novelty for their main results. Finally, lack of *theoretical* support for their main claims is also a major weakness (e.g., how or why a higher LR repairs isometry).

content.summary_of_the_paper: Recent work found that training the pruned network from scratch can achieve similar or even better performance than pruning a pretrained model. Even though recent studies questioned the value of filter pruning, this paper empirically shows that such a conclusion is due to suboptimal learning rate schedule settings.  Their results also confirmed such a hypothesis. The paper also provides a theoretical explanation through examining the dynamical isometry of networks in pruning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1- The paper looked at some existing findings on the importance of filter pruning and argued that it is not necessarily correct.
2- The paper builds up its argument by empirically showing that such a conclusion is due to suboptimal learning rate schedule settings and by changing the learning rate after pruning it showed the results are improved.
3- The paper also provides a theoretical explanation of why the learning rate should change in fine tuning step through examining the dynamical isometry of networks in pruning. 

Weakness: 
1- The paper promotes the idea of using the weights inherited from pruning as a kind of initialization for the following finetuning step. Even though I think it sounds reasonable, all experiments and analysis are based on L1-norm pruning which is a basic filter pruning method. 
2- I am wondering if the filter pruning method affects some findings and claims in the paper. For example it is highlighted in the paper that pruned models demand more finetuning epochs because inherited weights of a pruned model may pose it at a location NOT close to the final solution in the loss landscape. It would be really interesting to see if this is true for other existing methods. 
3- Through examining the dynamical isometry of networks in pruning, the paper showed that as the pruning ratio increases the mean JSV decreases and training becomes harder. In explaining LR effect on ImageNet, the paper only mentioned that changing the LR to 10^-2 improves the result since more dynamical isometry is damaged. I think showing the mean JSV for the imagenet will better provide support for the theoretical explanation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written and is easy to follow. Even though the paper doesn’t focus on improving existing filter pruning, it shed some light on the existing outcomes and argued both empirically and theoretically that there is room to improve.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper looked at some existing findings on the importance of filter pruning and argued that it is not necessarily correct. They provide both theoretical and experimental results that support their claim. The concern that I have is that the claims they made in the paper depend on the pruning method. But they only focus on L1-norm pruning which is a basic filter pruning method and other pruning techniques may not have the same outcome wrt closeness to the loss landscape. So I think some experimental results on other filter pruning methods are required and will improve the quality of the paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors refute the argument that "filter pruning is not worthwhile, and training small networks is superior" raised in previous papers.  First, the authors show that the existing methods have sufficiently high performance when the learning rate scheduler is set well through the L1-norm based pruning methods. To explain this phenomenon theoritically, the authors argue that filter pruning is the kinds of initialization and has worse properties than common initialization because it damages the mean Jacobian singular value (JSV). In other words, it is argued that the dynamical isometry of the pruned network is broken, and the reason why the existing pruned networks show higher performance when they use a higher learning rate.

As a method to repair damage, the authors propose a new pruning strategy called OrthP. First, the permuted kernel is orthogonalized in matrix form through QR decomposition. Then, the dynamical isometry is restored by leaving only the digonal components of R. As a result, the pruned network is efficiently trained without using a large learning rate. The authors prove that restoring the dynamical isometry is very helpful for performance improvement through experimental results using small network architectures and datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strength
. This paper raises a meaningful question about the fine-tuning process, which was rarely considered in the field of filter pruning. Most filter pruning algorithms, without a doubt, use a larger learning rate and pay the same training cost as pre-training. Therefore, the quest and hypothesis presented in this paper will be a meaningful insight for existing researchers.
. A simple but effective method addresses the problems posed by the authors. In other words, performance can be improved without worrying about cost, so it is considered to be practically worth introducing.

- Weakness
. The authors' arguments are interesting and well worth discussing. However, I don't think it has been sufficiently verified. The authors claim to be the first to theoretically analyze the fine-tuning problem of filter pruning. However, all hypotheses are being tested through experiments without rigorous proof.
. In addition, the authors are testing hypotheses and assumptions with datasets and architectures that are too small to claim to have been tested empirically.  In Tables 1, 2 and 3, this point is more emphasized compared to when the problems of the existing methods are verified. In other words, it is suspected that the experiment was not done even though it could be sufficiently tested.
. The authors used the most primive method, norm, as the filter pruning algorithm. More scoring methods and validation of NAS-based pruning methods also need to be done.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The authors claim that this paper is the first case of analyzing the trainability of a pruned network, but this is not true.
- The paper below shows the results of empirically analyzing the trainability of the pruned network through the condition number of the loss landscape, and the level of assumptions and experiments is not much different from that shown in this paper.
. Lee, Seunghyun, and Byung Cheol Song. "Ensemble Knowledge Guided Sub-network Search and Fine-tuning for Filter Pruning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.02651 (2022).
- Therefore, according to the authors' argument, the above paper will be the first case to analyze the trainability of a pruned network theorically. Of course, finding a subnetwork with better trainability and improving the trainability of a pruned network have different directions, but at least mention is necessary.
- The authors did not share the code directly, but since the proposed method is a simple QR decomposition, there is no difficulty in implementing it directly.
content.summary_of_the_review:
- Overall, this paper is well written, and motivation, problem statements and solutions are well established. In particular, the method OrthP for improving trainability seems simple but effective.

- However, experiments to verify the proposed algorithm and hypothesys are too poor. I am not saying that this paper should be subjected to extensive experimentation like the existing filter pruning papers. Instead of proving the problems of the well-known and low-importance existing techniques, this paper needs to put more effort into proving the generality of the proposed method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper makes a strong case in defense of preserving the weights of a network after pruning. The authors reevaluate experiments in the literature saying otherwise by providing more time for the fine-tuning to converge and showing that this leads to better accuracy in comparison to using new weights. They explain that the additional time needed is due to the lack of dynamical isometry in the weight matrices, which would otherwise help training converge faster. With a correction to the weight matrices that brings them closer to dynamical isometry, they show that a shorter fine-tuning produces better results now.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- I like it very much that the starting point of this paper is reproducing the exact experiments from the work that the authors are questioning, rather than creating their own independent experiments.
- The discussion about fine-tuning and loss landscapes is well-developed and I could intuitively understand where they were taking us. 
- The merit of this paper is connecting the dots in the literature to question findings that could have mislead us for year to come - that is a great feat for such a hand-on paper.

Weaknesses:
- I am somewhat conflicted with the small number of repetitions for the experiments: 3 is so little! Are these experiments so computationally expensive that you could not have run more?
- The discussion about dynamical isometry is much shorter and a bit less intuitive. As someone who is not familiar with the topic, I must say that at best I got an educated guess about how that part of the paper.
- The literature review is mostly on point, but I would recommend that the authors include a more recent and extensive survey on the topic (see [1] below). Moreover, I have a hard time accepting a distinction between importance-based and penalty-based pruning because both walk mostly side-by-side. See, for example, the discussion about how weight decay influences gradient-based pruning in [2] below.

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.00554
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.02976
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The novelty of the paper is entirely on connecting the dots and revisiting prior work. It is a great empirical paper. With that said, a more intuitive discussion of dynamical isometry would be welcomed. If the authors could elaborate a bit more on that in their rebuttal to possibly improve the description in the paper, that would be greatly appreciated. 

I noticed the use of "sup-optimal" a few times in the text, such as in pages 5 and 6. Is that a typo for sub-optimal, or I am missing something?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper has a meaningful contribution, but I am concerned with the low number of repetitions in the experiments and I would appreciate a more accessible description of dynamical isometry.

content.title: Examining the Value of Neural Filter Pruning -- Retrospect and Prospect
content.abstract: Neural network filter pruning is one of the major methods in model compression and acceleration. Despite the remarkable progress in the past several years, there is an ongoing debate concerning the value of filter pruning -- Some works in 2019 argue that filter pruning is of no value since they found training the pruned network from scratch can achieve similar or even better performance than pruning a pretrained model. This argument fundamentally challenges the value of many filter pruning works. However, to date, the community has not formally responded to such acute questioning. In this paper, we present extensive empirical analyses to show the seeming contradiction is due to suboptimal learning rate schedule settings. We introduce more strict comparison setups and show filter pruning still has value within the same training epoch budgets. Apart from justifying the value of filter pruning empirically, we further examine the reason behind it and discover that the poor trainability caused by pruning is largely responsible for the sub-optimality of the learning rate schedule, thus calling for an urgent need to recover trainability after pruning. This paper does not target new SOTA performance of filter pruning. Instead, we focus on clarifying the existing mysteries in filter pruning towards a better understanding.
